extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary aesthetics, poetry, and fine art
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotelian and classical-aesthetic criteria for judging poetry and fine art (ends, functions, audience, and formal requirements). Useful for literary criticism, aesthetics courses, or guiding creative practice informed by classical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the universal in the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry must present particulars that are 'representative of a class' — persons of poetry should be 'clothed with generic attributes' so that the universal truth shines through the individual; 'an involution of the universal in the individual.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge (reading Aristotle) warns these class characteristics are 'so modified and particularised' in each character that individuality remains strong. The universal is not a single abstract truth but the set of truths that meet in the individual; the poet seizes a concrete fact and transfigures it so the higher truth appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of fine art: pleasure (rational enjoyment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of the fine arts is to give pleasure (πρὸς ἡδονήν) or 'rational enjoyment' (πρὸς διαγωγήν), distinguishing fine arts from 'useful' arts whose ends are material or subordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle contrasts fine arts with useful arts; art's proper end is pleasurable and linked to leisure/schole. This pleasure is the distinctive goal of art and not merely incidental useful effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality/rank of pleasure: higher vs lower pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures produced by art differ in quality: there are 'harmless' pastime pleasures (ἀνάπαυσις/παιδιά) and elevated, noble pleasures associated with scholé and rational enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle (via examples in music and comedy) distinguishes amusement for children or pastime from aesthetic delight proper. Critics should evaluate whether an artwork affords the higher, contemplative pleasure or only a lower recreational pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness of subject determines artistic status (tragedy vs comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates a 'serious action' (πράξεως σπουδαίας) concerned with the supreme good and is a serious art; comedy is a sportive pastime with a lower pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By Aristotle's logic, works treating serious actions aim at the higher kind of pleasure and moral import; evaluating genre should account for whether the work fulfills the seriousness appropriate to its form (e.g., tragedy should not be reduced to comic or merely entertaining effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic enjoyment proceeds primarily from emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine art's main appeal is to the feelings rather than to the intellect; aesthetic enjoyment is an emotional delight (a 'glow of feeling') akin to, but distinct from, speculative thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique should attend to the emotional effect produced. While cognition and recognition can contribute (the 'pleasure of knowledge'), the proper aesthetic impact is emotional and empathetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of art judged by the spectator's pleasurable impression (ideal spectator)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work's end and perfection are known by the hedonistic effect it produces in the percipient; art is subordinated to the receptive activity of the spectator, not the maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle appeals to an 'ideal' cultivated public or a man of sound aesthetic instincts (ὁ χαρίεις) as the standard of taste. Evaluation should appeal to the cultivated listener/viewer rather than mere specialist technicians or vulgar popular taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive function criterion: each art must fulfill its characteristic emotional function
rubrics_metrics.description: Each kind of poetry carries a distinctive pleasure (e.g., tragedy has the inherent capacity to call forth pity and fear); the test of merit is the degree to which the work fulfills this distinctive function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules for plot, character, recognition, etc., arise from this primary requirement. Assessments should check whether formal elements are arranged to produce the characteristic emotional response (pity/fear in tragedy, appropriate pleasures in other genres).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/teleological completion: matter impressed with artistic form
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of artistic production is achieved when the process (γένεσις) is complete—when matter (ὕλη) has been impressed with artistic form (εἶδος) and potential is actualized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This teleological criterion emphasizes formal realization and completeness: judges should consider whether the work's material has been fully and properly shaped by artistic form, not merely its external effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective grounding of subjective pleasure (common human nature as validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though judged by subjective pleasure, that feeling is 'deeply grounded in human nature' and thereby acquires a kind of objective validity; a cultivated public is presumed to share appropriate responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators rely on shared human sympathies and trained aesthetic judgment. The 'man of taste' functions as a standard — critique should argue how a work's effects correspond to broadly human, cultivated responses rather than idiosyncratic moods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's possible moral/instructional function
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional view: poetry has a direct moral purpose; the poet acts as teacher ('poetry is a kind of elementary philosophy'), giving pleasurable instruction in character, emotion, and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical authorities (Homer, Plutarch, Strabo) regarded poetry as ethical education for youth and the masses. Evaluation can include whether a poem instructs or improves morals and whether it functions as a 'preparatory school of philosophy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's aim toward the audience rather than self-enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: In Greek thought the artist's end is not the inward satisfaction of creation but the pleasure of the spectator; the artist 'works not for himself but for others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern Romantic notions of art-as-self-realization differ; critics working with Aristotelian premises should prioritize the effect on and duties to the public when judging artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering to popular weakness (integrity of genre-function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists should not gratify the weakness of the audience by violating the proper function of the genre (e.g., making tragic plots end happily to please audiences undermines the characteristic tragic pleasure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should note instances where works sacrifice their distinctive end to popular tastes; such compromises may produce incidental pleasure but fail to fulfil the art's essential function.
